meta.title: SporeNet — The path to restoring ecosystems
meta.description: Restoring underground mycorrhizal networks in Kazakhstan's burned forests.

hero.title: SporeNet
hero.subtitle: The path to restoring ecosystems
hero.lead: Wildfires don't only burn trees — they destroy the underground mycorrhizal network that lets a forest live as one organism. SporeNet brings that network back.

problem.title: A forest is more than its trees
problem.lead: Beneath every healthy forest lies an invisible web of fungi — the mycorrhizal network — exchanging nutrients between trees, warning them of threats, and helping seedlings survive their first years. When wildfires sweep through Kazakhstan, this underground internet burns with the trees.

cards.title: Burned forests in Kazakhstan
cards.text: Over the last decade, wildfires have damaged hundreds of thousands of hectares across the country's northern and eastern forest belts.

cards.title: The hidden casualty
cards.text: After fire, the mycorrhizal layer is destroyed in the top 10–15 cm of soil — exactly where new seedlings need it most.

cards.title: Recovery without fungi
cards.text: Without mycorrhiza, new trees grow up to 3× slower and survive at much lower rates. Reforestation efforts fail silently.

solution.title: Reseeding the underground
solution.lead: SporeNet develops region-adapted mycorrhizal inoculants — living spore blends matched to the trees of Kazakhstan's forests. We work with local nurseries and reforestation teams to restore the network alongside the trees.

steps.title: 1. Sample
steps.text: We collect native fungal strains from surviving forest patches and isolate species that pair with local pines, birches and firs.

steps.title: 2. Cultivate
steps.text: Strains are propagated on substrate in low-cost lab conditions, producing inoculant ready for field use.

steps.title: 3. Inoculate
steps.text: Seedlings are dipped or soil-treated before planting, so each young tree starts life already connected to the network.

steps.title: 4. Monitor
steps.text: We track survival, growth and soil health to prove that restored mycelia accelerate forest recovery.
